h.select_rule: Discard any hypothesis whose condition is the edited field's own current value, or whose condition merely disables or disconnects the edited component. From the rest, keep 10 with distinct mechanisms and field pairs, favouring those where an informed expert could plausibly bet on either direction.
h.strategy: Two patterns are banned because experts find them obvious: (1) conditioning on the current value of the same field being edited, which just restates that upgrading a weak setting helps more than upgrading a strong one; (2) conditions that make the edited component unused, unreachable or inert. Instead, each hypothesis must link two DIFFERENT fields that interact through a non-trivial mechanism, such as substitution between parallel routes, a capacity already supplied elsewhere, one part acting as a bottleneck for another, or interference that turns a usually helpful edit harmful. No condition setting may appear in more than two hypotheses. Use the gaps and negated assumptions as the source of each idea. In each 'why', name the mechanism and explain why the opposite direction is also a priori plausible.

hyps.why: A 3x3 conv already feeding node 3 from node 1 supplies spatial capacity at the output sum, so a parallel 3x3 on 2->3 adds partly redundant features.
An identity 0->3 turns the deep conv path into a residual branch that optimizes easily, amplifying the value of a conv on 2->3.
Extra serial depth on 1->2 is well conditioned only when an identity path to the output exists.
When 1->2 carries a learned 3x3 map, a pooled 0->2 term is only minor additive smoothing at node 2, so the edit is less harmful.
Making node 1 an input copy costs little when the 1->3 conv still applies a learned transform downstream.
When node 3 already receives a 3x3 from node 2, a conv on 0->3 adds redundant learned features and forgoes the identity shortcut.
If edge 4 already carries an identity-like path into node 3, a second identity on 0->3 over-weights the raw input and adds little gradient benefit.
A learned conv on 0->3 dominates node 3, so a pooled 1->3 term is a mild smoothing and costs less.
When 0->2 is already a 3x3 conv, disabling node 1 loses less because node 2 still receives learned features.
If node 2's other input is only pooled, a skip from node 1 brings in its possibly learned features and avoids an all-pooled node 2.
